news.title: Good Future and Chung Shan Medical University Hospital publish breast cancer CTC study in MDPI Diseases
news.summary: A newly published MDPI paper showed that CSV+ CTCs measured on Good Future's automated negative selection platform may support metastatic-risk stratification and recurrence monitoring in breast cancer.
body: Good Future and Chung Shan Medical University Hospital have published a breast-cancer circulating tumor cell study in MDPI Diseases.
The study used the Chiline CATCH automated negative selection platform and EpCAM plus CSV as the main identification markers.
The paper reported that CSV+ CTC counts, rather than EpCAM+ counts, were associated with higher metastatic risk.
CSV+ CTC counts also outperformed conventional serum tumor markers and were associated with worse progression-free survival at higher levels.
These findings highlight the value of an automated negative selection platform in preserving clinically meaningful CTC phenotypes.

news.title: Liquid biopsy and CTC testing in precision cancer care
news.summary: An overview of circulating tumor cells, common enrichment approaches, and the role of CTC information in cancer-related research and follow-up.
body: Liquid biopsy refers to the analysis of tumor-associated material found in body fluids. Circulating tumor cells are one such source of information and can be studied for cell morphology, protein markers, and molecular characteristics.

CTC workflows generally include enrichment, staining, imaging, and interpretation. Positive-selection methods capture cells that express selected markers, while negative-selection methods remove unwanted blood cells and may preserve a broader range of CTC phenotypes.
CTC testing remains an adjunct to established clinical assessment. Results should be interpreted together with pathology, imaging, medical history, and other laboratory findings.

share.title: Breast cancer CTC paper summary: what the automated negative selection platform revealed
share.summary: See why CSV+ CTCs stood out in this study and what the results suggest for metastatic-risk stratification and recurrence monitoring.
body: This paper focused on CSV+ circulating tumor cells in breast cancer and used Good Future’s automated negative selection platform to enrich and evaluate them.
The study found that CSV+ CTCs, rather than EpCAM+ CTCs, were associated with higher metastatic risk.
More than 4.5 CSV+ CTCs per 2 mL of blood showed strong specificity for identifying higher-risk patients.
CSV+ CTCs also outperformed CA 15-3, CA 125, and CEA, and the combined use improved risk stratification further.
The paper reinforces the value of negative selection in preserving clinically meaningful CTC phenotypes.

share.title: Circulating tumor cells in precision cancer care
share.summary: Learn how CTCs enter the bloodstream and why CTC testing is being studied as an adjunct for cancer-risk assessment and follow-up.
body: Circulating tumor cells, or CTCs, are cells that detach from a primary or metastatic tumor and enter the bloodstream. Because they can be collected through a blood draw, they provide a way to study tumor-associated cells over time.

A CTC workflow typically includes enrichment, immunofluorescence staining, imaging, and interpretation. Cell morphology and combinations of markers are reviewed together rather than treating any single signal as definitive.

Research has explored CTCs for risk stratification, treatment monitoring, and recurrence surveillance. Their clinical significance depends on cancer type, assay method, and the patient's broader clinical context.
CTC testing is supplementary and does not replace pathology, imaging, or diagnosis by a qualified physician.

share.title: How negative selection helps preserve a broader range of CTC phenotypes
share.summary: Learn how red blood cell removal, white blood cell identification, and magnetic separation can enrich candidate CTCs without relying on a single tumor marker.
body: CTC enrichment methods use either physical properties, such as cell size, or biological properties, such as surface-marker expression. Each approach has trade-offs because tumor cells are heterogeneous and may change phenotype during disease progression.

Positive selection captures cells that express a predefined tumor-associated marker. It can be effective when marker expression is stable, but cells with low or absent expression may be underrepresented.

Good Future uses a negative-selection workflow. Red blood cells are removed first, white blood cells are identified with specific antibodies, and magnetic separation is used to reduce unwanted blood cells. The remaining cell population can then proceed to immunofluorescence staining, automated imaging, and review.

By not requiring every candidate cell to express one capture marker, negative selection may reduce marker-related cell loss. Final interpretation still depends on cell morphology, marker combinations, quality controls, and clinical context.

share.title: Why epithelial and mesenchymal CTC phenotypes both matter
share.summary: CTCs are biologically heterogeneous. Reviewing epithelial and mesenchymal markers together may provide a more complete view than relying on a single signal.
body: Circulating tumor cells can display epithelial, mesenchymal, or mixed phenotypes. This heterogeneity is partly related to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a biological process studied in tumor invasion and metastasis.

A workflow that relies only on an epithelial marker may underrepresent cells with reduced epithelial-marker expression. Including mesenchymal-associated markers can broaden the phenotypes available for review.
Marker expression alone does not establish malignancy. Cell morphology, multiple staining signals, assay controls, and the patient's clinical information must be considered together.
Research continues to evaluate how specific CTC phenotypes relate to prognosis and treatment response across different cancer types.

share.title: From a 2 mL blood sample to a CTC report in about five business days
share.summary: Follow the Good Future workflow from specimen collection and cell enrichment to immunofluorescence imaging and report delivery.
body: Good Future's current CTC testing workflow begins with a 2 mL blood sample. Fasting is not required, but collection, storage, and transportation instructions should be followed to protect specimen quality.

At the laboratory, the sample undergoes preprocessing, cell enrichment, immunofluorescence staining, automated microscopy, and image review. These steps are designed to reduce background blood cells and preserve candidate cells for interpretation.
Reports are generally delivered in about five business days and include a result summary, representative cell images, and phenotype-related observations.
The report is intended to support discussion with qualified healthcare professionals. It does not replace pathology, imaging, or other standard diagnostic procedures.
